question: A console program is over when main reaches its last line. A Swing program's main builds a window, shows it, and then reaches its last line too. What happens next?
correct: The window stays open and the program waits for events such as clicks
incorrect: The program ends, and the window closes along with it
main starts again from its first line to keep the window up
main pauses at setVisible(true) until the window is closed
feedback: Showing a window starts Swing's own thread, which keeps the program alive after main has finished. From then on nothing runs top to bottom: the program sits waiting, and a piece of your code runs whenever the user does something. main is not re-run, and setVisible(true) returns straight away rather than waiting for the window to close.

question: A user clicks a JButton, or presses the space bar while the button has focus. Swing reports both as the same kind of event. Which listener interface receives it?
correct: ActionListener
incorrect: KeyListener
WindowListener
MouseMotionListener
feedback: A button turns 'the user activated me', by mouse or by keyboard, into one ActionEvent and delivers it to its ActionListeners. That is why you listen for the action rather than for raw mouse or key events: a KeyListener would miss the mouse, and a mouse listener would miss the keyboard. WindowListener is for the frame itself (opening, closing, minimising).

question: Match each Swing class to the job it does in a window.

pairs.definition: A top-level window with a title bar, able to appear on screen by itself
An invisible container that groups other components under its own layout manager
Text or an icon that the user can read but cannot edit
One line of text that the user can type and the program can read back
A control that fires an action event each time the user presses it

feedback: A JFrame is the outer window; everything else lives inside one. A JPanel is the workhorse for organising a window, because each panel can have a different layout manager. A JLabel only displays, a JTextField accepts a line of typing (read it with getText()), and a JButton exists to fire action events at its listeners.

question: Arrange these lines, first to last, so that the window appears once and is already the right size for its button.
feedback: The frame has to exist before anything can be added to it. pack() sizes the window to fit the preferred sizes of whatever it contains, so it comes after the components are added: packing an empty frame gives a window sized for nothing. setVisible(true) comes last so that the user sees one finished window rather than a tiny one that then jumps to size.

question: A small Swing program builds a JFrame holding one JButton. Match each call to what goes wrong when that one call is left out and nothing replaces it.

pairs.definition: No window shows up on screen at all
A window shows up, collapsed to little more than its title bar
Closing the window hides it, yet the program keeps running
The button can be pressed, yet pressing it changes nothing

feedback: A JFrame starts out invisible and with a size of zero, so it needs both a size (pack(), or setSize) and setVisible(true). The default close operation is HIDE_ON_CLOSE: the window vanishes but the program is still running in the background until you stop it, which is why almost every small program asks for EXIT_ON_CLOSE. A button with no listener still animates when pressed; there is simply no code for it to call.

question: NPC: A listener is an object waiting to be called
intro: Zoya sets a small brass bell on the bench and wires a push-button to it. "A button knows nothing about bells," they say. "All it knows is a list of objects to call when it is pressed."

steps.say: A button does nothing by itself. You hand it a listener: an object with one method, actionPerformed. A lambda can stand in for it, because ActionListener has exactly one abstract method.

beats.say: A button does nothing by itself. You hand it a listener: an object with one method, actionPerformed.
ActionListener has exactly one abstract method, so a lambda can stand in for it. The part after the arrow is the body of actionPerformed.

steps.say: Registering is not ringing. addActionListener only stores the listener in the button's list. The lambda body has not run.

check.prompt: Straight after addActionListener, what is bell.strikes?
check.answer: 0: nothing has called the listener yet
wrong: It depends on the button's text
check.why: addActionListener just remembers the listener. The body runs later, when something calls actionPerformed.

steps.say: Each click makes Swing call actionPerformed once. I can make the same call myself, with no window at all. Two calls, two strikes.

beats.say: Each click makes Swing call actionPerformed once. I can make the same call myself, with no window at all:
Two calls, two strikes. That is event-driven programming: you write the handler now, and something else decides when it runs, and how many times.

outro: "The next monster has wired up a listener of its own," Zoya says. "Count the calls, not the lines."

question: The listener here is called directly, the same way a button would call it on each click. What does this print?
feedback: Creating the lambda runs nothing, so the first println still sees 0. Each call to actionPerformed runs the body once, adding 2: three calls give 6. The tempting wrong answers are 2 (as if defining the listener ran it) and 0 twice (as if a lambda could not change the object it captured).

feedback_template: The addActionListener line itself adds nothing to score: it only registers the handler. Each of the {{n}} clicks then runs the body once, adding {{step}}, so score goes from {{start}} to {{expected}}.

correct: count is a local variable, and a lambda may not reassign a local it captures
incorrect: count++ produces a value, and an ActionListener lambda has to return nothing
The parameter e is declared, but the body of the lambda does not make use of it
A lambda needs a cast to ActionListener before addActionListener will accept it
feedback: A lambda can read a local variable only if that variable is effectively final, because the handler may run long after the method that declared the local has returned. The fix is to keep the number somewhere that outlives main: a field, or better an object such as a model (model.count++ compiles, since the variable model is never reassigned, only the object it points to changes). An unused parameter is fine, count++ is a legal statement in a void lambda, and no cast is needed.

question:
Which statements about this line are true?

button.addActionListener(e -> label.setText("Hi"));
correct: The lambda body runs each time the button is clicked
Running this line leaves the label's text as it was
e is the ActionEvent object that describes the click
A lambda fits because ActionListener has one abstract method
incorrect: The listener is removed once it has handled its first click
The line waits here until the user has clicked the button
feedback: The line registers a handler and returns immediately; nothing is displayed and nothing waits. From then on Swing calls the body once per click, passing an ActionEvent (which can tell you, for example, which button fired). A listener stays registered until you remove it. The lambda is shorthand for an object implementing ActionListener, which works because that interface has a single abstract method, actionPerformed.

question: doClick() presses a button from code, just as a user's click would. One listener is registered on two buttons; getActionCommand() gives the text of the button that fired the event. What does this print?
correct:
No
Yes
No
feedback: Nothing prints while the buttons are created or the listener is registered. Output appears only when a button fires, in the order the clicks happen: No, Yes, No. The order in which the buttons were created or registered (Yes first) is irrelevant. The event object is how one shared listener finds out which button it is being called for.

feedback_template: A button keeps a list of listeners, and addActionListener appends to it every time it is called, so this button ends up with {{k}} listeners. Each click calls every listener on the list: {{n}} clicks give {{expected}}. This is a real bug: it appears when the registering line sits in a method that runs more than once, and the symptom is a handler that seems to fire several times per click.

question: A JLabel named msg is on screen. Write the statement a handler would use to change its text to Done.
correct: msg.setText("Done");
msg.setText("Done")
feedback: setText replaces what the label displays; Swing repaints the label shortly afterwards. Its partner getText() reads the current text back. Assigning to the label (msg = "Done") does not compile: msg is a JLabel, not a String.

question: The user has typed 12 into a text field. What do these lines print?
feedback: getText() always returns a String, whatever the user typed. String + 1 is concatenation, giving 121. Only after Integer.parseInt has turned the text into an int does + mean addition, giving 13. Every number that comes out of a text field has to be parsed before you can calculate with it.

question: A handler runs Integer.parseInt(field.getText()) and the user has typed abc. Nothing in the handler catches the NumberFormatException. What does the user experience?
correct: The rest of that handler is skipped, but the window stays open and usable
incorrect: The window closes, because an uncaught exception ends the program
A dialog box appears, showing the exception and its stack trace
parseInt gives back 0 for text it cannot read, so the handler carries on
feedback: The thread that runs listeners survives an exception thrown by one of them: it prints the stack trace to the console and moves on to the next event. A user who started the program by double-clicking sees no console, so from their side the button simply did nothing. That silence is why a handler should catch NumberFormatException itself and say something useful in a label or dialog. parseInt does not return 0 for bad input; it throws.

question: Arrange the body of a Deposit button's handler, first line to last, so that the label ends up showing the balance including the new deposit.
feedback: Each line needs what the line before it produced: the text must be read before it can be parsed, the int must exist before it can be deposited, and the label must be refreshed after the model has changed, or it would show the old balance. Read the view, update the model, refresh the view: most handlers have this shape.

question: Why do Swing programs hand positioning to a layout manager instead of giving each component exact pixel coordinates?
correct: Positions are worked out again when the window is resized or fonts differ
incorrect: Pixel coordinates are not available, since setBounds was removed from Swing
A component placed by coordinates is unable to receive click events
A layout manager paints components faster than fixed coordinates allow
feedback: A layout manager is a rule ('buttons in a row', 'a four by four grid') rather than a list of positions, and Swing re-applies the rule whenever the container changes size. Fixed coordinates look right on one screen, with one font, at one window size. They are still legal (setLayout(null) plus setBounds), they do not affect events, and speed is not the issue.

question: Match each layout choice to how it arranges the components in a container.

pairs.definition: Edge strips around a middle area that takes whatever space is left over
Components at their preferred sizes, left to right, wrapping to a new row when one fills
Rows and columns of equal-sized cells, each component stretched to fill its cell
Nothing is arranged for you; each component needs its bounds set by hand

feedback: BorderLayout suits a whole window (toolbar on top, status bar below, content in the middle). FlowLayout suits a short row of buttons and is what a new JPanel uses by default. GridLayout suits keypads and boards where every cell should match. A null layout gives full control and no help: nothing moves when the window is resized.

question: A BorderLayout has {{1}} regions. A component added without naming a region lands in {{2}}. A component in NORTH or SOUTH is stretched to the full width of the container but keeps its preferred {{3}}.
feedback: The five regions are NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST and CENTER. NORTH and SOUTH get the full width and their preferred height; EAST and WEST get their preferred width and the height that remains; CENTER takes everything left over, which is why the main content goes there. add(component) with no region means CENTER. A JFrame's content pane uses BorderLayout unless you change it.

correct: Only Load, filling the whole window
incorrect: Only Save, filling the whole window
Save on the left and Load on the right
Save above Load, each with half the height
feedback: With no region named, both buttons go to CENTER, and each BorderLayout region displays one component: the most recent one. Save is still inside the frame, but it is never given any space, so it cannot be seen. Buttons side by side or stacked would need a different layout manager, or a JPanel holding both placed in the region.

question: A panel with a BorderLayout (no gaps) is 600 pixels wide and {{H}} pixels tall. A toolbar with a preferred height of {{n}} is in NORTH, a status bar with a preferred height of {{s}} is in SOUTH, and a text area is in CENTER. How many pixels tall is the text area?
feedback_template: NORTH and SOUTH are given exactly their preferred heights ({{n}} and {{s}}) and the full width. CENTER takes what remains: {{H}} minus both, which is {{expected}}. The text area's own preferred size plays no part, and the width of 600 does not enter into the height at all. When the window grows taller, all of the extra goes to CENTER.

question: A frame uses BorderLayout, with a large text area in CENTER. You want OK, Cancel and Help side by side along the bottom edge. Which approach works?
correct: Put the three buttons in a JPanel, then add that panel to SOUTH
incorrect: Add each button to SOUTH in turn, and the region lines them up in a row
Add the buttons to WEST, SOUTH and EAST so that they sit along the bottom
Switch the frame to FlowLayout, so that SOUTH is able to hold three buttons
feedback: A BorderLayout region shows one component, but that component can be a JPanel with a layout manager and children of its own. A panel (FlowLayout by default) holding the three buttons, placed in SOUTH, gives a button row under the text area. Adding the buttons to SOUTH one after another leaves only Help showing; WEST and EAST are the side strips, not the bottom corners; and a FlowLayout has no SOUTH at all. Nesting panels is how real windows are built.

question: NPC: In a GridLayout, the rows win
intro: Zoya is fitting rune-keys into a brass keypad frame. "GridLayout is the simplest layout manager there is," they say, "and it still surprises people the first time a key too many goes in."

steps.say: Two rows, three columns: six equal cells. Components fill them in the order you add them, left to right, then top to bottom.

beats.say: new GridLayout(2, 3) asks for 2 rows and 3 columns: six cells, every one the same size. Components fill them in the order you add them, left to right, then top to bottom.
Each button is stretched to fill its cell. Its preferred size is ignored.

steps.say: Now I add buttons 7 and 8. No cell is free. GridLayout does not hide them and does not start a third row. When the row count is not zero, it keeps the rows and ignores the column count you gave.

check.prompt: Eight buttons in a GridLayout(2, 3). How many columns appear?
wrong: 3, and the two extras are hidden
3, and a third row is added
check.why: The rows are fixed at 2, so the columns grow: 8 divided by 2, rounded up, is 4.

steps.say: To fix the columns instead, pass 0 for the rows: new GridLayout(0, 3) means three columns and as many rows as it takes. Either way the cells stay equal: each one is the panel's width divided by the number of columns.

beats.say: To fix the columns instead, pass 0 for the rows:

beats.code: new GridLayout(0, 3)   // 3 columns, as many rows as needed

beats.say: Either way the cells stay equal: each is as wide as the panel's width divided by the number of columns.

outro: "A monster ahead has crammed too many keys into its grid," Zoya says. "Divide by the rows and round up."

question: A panel is created with new GridLayout({{r}}, {{c}}), and then {{n}} buttons are added to it. How many columns of buttons appear on screen?
feedback_template: {{n}} buttons do not fit in {{r}} rows of {{c}}. When the row count is not zero, GridLayout keeps the {{r}} rows and treats the column count as a suggestion: it uses as many columns as it takes, {{n}} divided by {{r}} rounded up, which is {{expected}}. No button is hidden and no extra row is added.

question: A panel is created with new GridLayout(0, {{c}}), and then {{n}} buttons are added to it. How many rows of buttons appear on screen?
feedback_template: A row count of 0 means 'as many rows as needed', so the {{c}} columns are fixed and the rows grow: {{n}} divided by {{c}}, rounded up, is {{expected}}. If the last row is not full, its remaining cells are simply left empty.

question: A panel {{W}} pixels wide uses new GridLayout({{r}}, {{c}}) with no gaps and holds exactly {{total}} buttons. One button says OK and another says Open Recent File. How many pixels wide is the OK button?
feedback_template: Every GridLayout cell is the same size, and each component is stretched to fill its cell, so the length of a button's text makes no difference. The {{W}} pixels are shared equally by {{c}} columns: {{expected}} each. (In a FlowLayout the two buttons would have had different widths, because FlowLayout respects preferred sizes.)

question: A JPanel that fills the window holds five buttons in a single row, using the panel's default FlowLayout. The user drags the window narrower until three buttons fit across. What happens to the other two?
correct: They wrap onto a second row, still at their preferred size
incorrect: All five shrink equally so that they still share the one row
They stay on the row and are cut off at the panel's right edge
They are stacked on top of the third button and hidden by it
feedback: FlowLayout works like words in a paragraph: each component keeps its preferred size, and when the next one does not fit on the row it starts a new row. Shrinking everything equally to share the space is what GridLayout does. Nothing is clipped or overlapped as long as the panel is tall enough for the extra row.

question: Swing calls every listener, and does all of its painting, on the event-dispatch thread (EDT). A program has three windows and twenty buttons with listeners. How many event-dispatch threads does it have?
correct: One, shared by every window and button
incorrect: Three, one for each open window
Twenty, one for each button's listener
None until a click, which starts a new one
feedback: There is a single EDT for the whole program. Events from every window join one queue, and the EDT takes them one at a time: it runs a handler to the end, then paints, then takes the next event. One thread makes Swing simple to reason about (two handlers never run at the same moment), and it is also the reason one slow handler stalls every window at once.

question: These lines run in main. isEventDispatchThread() reports whether the code calling it is running on the EDT. What is printed?
correct:
false
true
feedback: main runs on the program's main thread, which is not the EDT, so the first line prints false. invokeLater does not run the lambda itself: it puts the lambda in the EDT's queue, and the EDT runs it a moment later, so inside the lambda the answer is true. This is how code that starts in main gets GUI work done on the right thread.

question: Why do Swing programs usually build their window inside SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> ...) rather than directly in main?
correct: Swing components are not thread-safe, so they are created and changed on the EDT
incorrect: invokeLater holds the build back until the operating system has a window ready
invokeLater starts a fresh thread for each window so a slow handler blocks just one
main is a static method, and Swing components can be created from instance code
feedback: Swing's components are written on the assumption that one thread, the EDT, touches them. Listeners already run there; main does not. Building the window from main means two threads can be working on the same components at once, which produces rare, unrepeatable glitches. invokeLater hands the building code to the EDT. It creates no new threads and has nothing to do with the operating system or with static.

question: invokeLater adds a task to the end of the EDT's queue, and the EDT finishes the task it is running before it starts the next. What does this print?
correct:
A
C
B
feedback: The outer task prints A, then queues the inner task, then carries on and prints C. Only when the outer task has returned does the EDT take the next item from its queue and print B. 'Later' means 'after what is running now has finished', not 'right here'. A handler that asks for a repaint is in the same position: the repaint happens after the handler returns.

question: Arrange the life of a Swing program from launch to the end of its first button click, first to last.
items: main hands the window-building code to invokeLater, and main returns
The EDT runs that code: the window is built and shown
The EDT waits, with nothing in its queue
The user clicks the button, and a click event joins the queue
The EDT calls the button's actionPerformed
The handler returns; the EDT repaints and goes back to waiting
feedback: Set-up happens once, and after that the program spends nearly all of its time waiting. Your code runs in short bursts, each started by an event and each running on the EDT. The window cannot be repainted until the handler has returned, which is why the last two steps come in that order.

question: NPC: The frozen window
intro: Ada clicks a button labelled Brew on a little potion-timer program, then tries to drag its window aside. It will not budge. "Good," she says. "It is broken in exactly the way I wanted to show you."

steps.say: Every listener runs on one thread: the event-dispatch thread, the EDT. The same thread repaints the window, and it does one job at a time.

beats.say: Here is the handler behind that button:
Every listener runs on one thread: the event-dispatch thread, or EDT. That same thread repaints the window, and it does one job at a time.

steps.say: setText does not paint anything. It stores the new text and adds a repaint request to the EDT's queue. But the EDT is still busy inside this handler.

check.prompt: During the 5 seconds of slowBrew(), does the user see Brewing...?
check.answer: No: painting waits until the handler returns
wrong: Yes: painting has a thread of its own
check.why: The repaint is queued behind the handler that requested it. By the time it runs, the text is already Done.

steps.say: So for five seconds the window is frozen: no repainting, no dragging, no response. Clicks made meanwhile are not lost. They wait in the queue and run afterwards, one after another.

beats.say: So for five seconds the window is frozen: no repainting, no response to anything. The user never sees Brewing... at all.
Clicks made during the freeze are not lost. They wait in the queue and are handled afterwards, one after another.
The cure: handlers must return quickly. Slow work goes to a background thread (Swing's helper for that is SwingWorker), and only the quick step of showing the result comes back to the EDT.

outro: "The next monster has an impatient user," Ada says. "Work out how long its window stays frozen."

question: A button's handler does slow work on the EDT and takes {{s}} seconds to return. An impatient user clicks the button {{k}} times within the first second. For about how many seconds in total is the window frozen?
feedback_template: The extra clicks are not thrown away and do not run in parallel: they wait in the EDT's queue. One thread runs the handler {{k}} times, one after another, at {{s}} seconds each, so the window is unresponsive for about {{expected}} seconds. Clicking again makes a frozen program worse, never better.

question: A Load button's handler reads a huge file, and the window freezes for ten seconds each time. Which change cures the freeze?
correct: Read the file on a background thread, then update the label back on the EDT
incorrect: Wrap the file-reading code in SwingUtilities.invokeLater so that it runs later
Call repaint() just before reading the file, so the window is redrawn first
Move the file-reading code out of the lambda and into a separate named method
feedback: The window freezes because the EDT is busy, so the slow work has to leave the EDT; SwingWorker exists for exactly this. invokeLater is the tempting wrong answer: it runs the code later, but still on the EDT, so the freeze just moves. repaint() only queues a request that cannot be served until the handler returns, and a named method called from the handler runs on the same thread as the handler.

question: Which of these jobs belong on the event-dispatch thread?
correct: Changing a label's text with setText
Creating the JFrame and its buttons
Reading a text field with getText
incorrect: Downloading a file from a web server
Sorting several million records
Sleeping three seconds between two frames
feedback: The rule has two halves. Anything that touches Swing components (creating them, reading them, changing them) belongs on the EDT, because components are not thread-safe. Anything slow (networks, big files, heavy computation, sleeping) belongs off it, because while the EDT is busy the window cannot repaint or respond. For timed animation Swing offers javax.swing.Timer, which calls a listener on the EDT at intervals without any sleeping.

question: NPC: Three jobs, three places
intro: Zoya holds up a counting-golem whose tally is written in chalk on its own face. "Ask it the count and you have to read its face," they say. "Wipe the face and the count is gone. Let me show you the same mistake in Swing."

steps.say: This counter works, but the count lives inside the label's text. The only way to learn the count is to read the screen: no window, no count, and no way to test it.

beats.say: This counter works, but look where the count lives: inside the label's text. That is the chalk on the golem's face.
The only way to learn the count is to read the screen. No window, no count, and so no way to test the counting.

steps.say: Move the data and its rules into a plain class with no Swing in it. That class is the model. The label and the button are the view: they show things and collect input, nothing more.

beats.say: Move the data and its rules into a plain class with no Swing in it. That class is the model.
The label and the button are the view: they show things and collect input, nothing more.

check.prompt: Counter has no idea a window exists. So who calls increment() when the button is clicked?
wrong: The label, when it is repainted
check.why: The model never reaches out to the GUI. A third piece, the controller, hears the event and calls the model.

steps.say: The controller is the go-between. It hears the event, tells the model to change, then refreshes the view from the model. The model never touches the view.

beats.say: The controller is the go-between. It hears the event, tells the model to change, then refreshes the view from the model.
The model never touches the view. That is what lets you test it, or put a different window on top of it, without changing a line.

outro: "Next you will be handed a single line of code," Zoya says, "and asked which of the three places it belongs in."

question:
A Swing tip calculator is built as MVC. Where does this line belong?

double tip = bill * percent / 100.0;
correct: Model
incorrect: View
Controller
The main method
feedback: The line is a rule of the problem itself: it would be just as true in a console program or a phone app. Rules and data belong in the model. The view only displays the result, the controller only decides when to ask for it, and main just wires the three together. A quick test: if a line mentions no Swing class and would survive a complete change of interface, it is model code.

question: When the user clicks Add, the {{1}} receives the event, asks the {{2}} to update the total, and then tells the {{3}} to display the new value.
feedback: The controller is the listener code: it hears the event and coordinates. The model owns the total and the rules for changing it. The view is the labels, fields and buttons that show the result. Calls flow from the controller to the other two; the model never calls the view.

question: InventoryModel is the model class of an MVC program. Which of these lines, found inside it, show that the separation has broken down?
correct: stockLabel.setText("" + stock);
JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Out of stock");
incorrect: if (amount < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
private int stock;
return stock < 5;
feedback: A model holds data and rules and knows nothing about how they are shown. Updating a label and popping up a dialog (JOptionPane is Swing's ready-made dialog class) are both display work, so they belong to the view, triggered by the controller. A private field, a rule such as 'stock is low below 5', and refusing a negative amount by throwing an exception are exactly what a model is for: the controller can catch that exception and decide how to tell the user.

question: No window is opened here: the code calls the controller's listener directly, five times. What does it print?
feedback: The listener runs five times, but the model's own rule refuses to go below zero: 3, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0. The answer is not -2, because the rule lives in the model and applies however lose() gets called. Notice that the whole check ran without a window or a mouse; that is what separating the logic buys you.

question: Why is a rule such as 'lives stop at zero' easier to check automatically when it lives in a model class rather than inside a button's listener?
correct: A test can create the model and call its methods with no window or clicks
incorrect: A model class runs on a thread of its own, so a test can watch it as the GUI runs
Listener lambdas are discarded by the compiler, so test code is unable to reach them
Swing classes are unable to be imported into a file that also contains test code
feedback: A model is an ordinary class: construct it, call lose() five times, compare getLeft() with 0. That takes a few lines and a few milliseconds. The same rule buried in a listener can be reached only by building the window and producing clicks. Models get no thread of their own, lambdas are compiled like any other code, and tests may import Swing; the point is that they should not have to.

question: A text field, a label, a model and a controller, with the user's typing and clicks simulated in code. What does this print?
feedback: First click: 7 parses, the model's sum becomes 7 and the label shows 7. Second click: x cannot be parsed, so parseInt throws before model.add runs; the catch block sets the label to ? and the model is untouched. Third click: 5 parses and the sum becomes 12. The label showed ? for a while, but the total was never lost, because the total lives in the model and not in the label.
